opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's necessary because these arguments are out there, and many of them are made in good faith by people I respect, including colleagues I've worked with for decades. If we just dismiss them, we're not doing our job as scientists. Science is about confronting the strongest version of the opposing view and seeing whether your position holds up.

There's also a practical reason. A lot of decision-makers, whether in government or in companies, hear these counterarguments, things like "AGI is centuries away," or "we'll just keep the AI under control because we built it," or "regulation will kill innovation," or "the benefits are so large we can't afford to slow down." If nobody carefully explains why those arguments don't hold, or why they don't justify ignoring the risks, then they become the default, and policy gets made on that basis.

And honestly, I went through this process myself. For a long time I didn't take catastrophic risks very seriously. I had my own reasons, some of them the same ones I now hear from others. It was only when I sat down and asked myself, "Okay, what is the actual argument here? Does it really show that we're safe?" that I realized most of them don't. Many of them, when you look closely, amount to "it will probably be fine." But "probably fine" isn't good enough when the downside could be the loss of human control, or something irreversible.

So the point of going through them one by one isn't to win a debate. It's to show that, given the uncertainty, and there is a lot of uncertainty, even among experts, the rational response is precaution. You don't need to be sure that disaster will happen. You need to recognize that you can't rule it out, and that the stakes are enormous. That's how we treat other risks in society, and I don't see why AI should be an exception.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scientists should not dismiss opposing arguments, but should confront their strongest versions and test whether their own position holds up. This presents individual engagement as necessary for intellectual honesty.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a question of intellectual honesty, first of all. When I started speaking publicly about these risks, I had spent most of my career as someone who was fairly dismissive of them. So I know from the inside what it feels like to hold the opposite view and to think that the people worrying were being a bit naive or science-fictional. If I just show up now and say "trust me, be worried," that's not going to convince anyone, and frankly it shouldn't.

What changed my mind was actually going through the arguments one by one. People say, "We're nowhere near human-level AI." Okay, well, let's look at the trajectory and ask what our uncertainty actually is. People say, "We can just unplug it." Okay, let's think about whether that's realistic once these systems are embedded in the economy and possibly more capable than us at persuasion. People say, "Intelligence doesn't imply bad intentions." Fine, but goals and intelligence are separate things, and we don't currently know how to reliably specify the goals. Each of these objections is reasonable on its face, and each of them, when I looked carefully, turned out to be much weaker than I had assumed.

So the second reason is that the counterarguments are where the real debate lives. If I dismiss them, I'm just doing the mirror image of what I used to do, which is dismiss the concerns. The scientific attitude is to say: here is the argument, here is why I don't think it holds up, and if you can show me where I'm wrong, I'll update. That's how we make progress on anything.

And the third reason is about the nature of the decision. We're talking about something potentially irreversible. When the stakes are that asymmetric, you don't need certainty that things will go badly to justify precaution. You need to show that you can't rule it out. So engaging with every argument against precaution is really a way of checking whether any of them actually gets us to "we can rule it out." And so far, I haven't found one that does. That's not a comfortable conclusion for me, but I think it's the honest one, and I'd rather people reach it by following the reasoning themselves than by taking my word for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls engaging with the arguments individually a matter of intellectual honesty and explains that dismissing counterarguments would repeat the mistake of dismissing the concerns.

astra-6.text:
Because if someone has an argument against taking precautions, we need to understand whether it’s a good argument. We could be wrong about some things. And if we’re asking society to make consequential decisions, we should be willing to examine the objections seriously, rather than just repeat that the risks are large.

But there’s also an asymmetry here. We don’t need certainty that something catastrophic will happen in order to take precautions. We need to consider how plausible it is, how severe the consequences would be, and what it would cost to reduce the risk. So an argument like “we don’t know whether these systems will become dangerous” is not, by itself, an argument for doing nothing. That uncertainty is part of what we have to reason about.

I think engaging with each argument helps us distinguish legitimate disagreements about what to do from reasons that don’t actually justify inaction. And it can help us find precautions that make sense even among people who have different views about the future.

r001.rationale: The response says we could be wrong and should examine objections seriously before making consequential decisions, framing engagement with each argument as necessary to reason honestly.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if we want people to act with precaution, we have to take their objections seriously. We can’t just say, “There’s a risk, therefore you should agree with us.” People have different beliefs about how the technology will develop, about the magnitude of the risks, and about the costs of taking precautions. We need to understand those disagreements and explain where we think the arguments go wrong—or revise our own views if they’re right.

And this matters because we need a collective response. It’s not enough for a few researchers to be convinced. We need the public and policymakers to understand why precaution makes sense even though there’s uncertainty. Uncertainty doesn’t mean we should do nothing; it means we should make decisions that take seriously the possibility of very bad outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says objections must be taken seriously and that we should revise our own views if they are right, clearly linking engagement with arguments to intellectual honesty.
